neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Theorem 17 first supplies a good time and a multiscale-good spatial interval; Proposition 28 is then iterated over O(log^2 T) short steps while shrinking only polylogarithmically, yielding time-zero energy control on the target block.

neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Time-zero renormalized energy forces almost every normalized consecutive gap to approach one, while a known zeta-zero gap result supplies a positive proportion bounded strictly below mean spacing.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: Smooth time-averaged energy control can be transferred to a terminal local block by selecting buffered spatial boundaries and iterating short-time monotonicity, after which nearest-neighbor statistics provide the contradiction.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The final obstruction uses an external theorem about zeta-zero gaps under the already implied Riemann hypothesis; this source does not reprove that statistical result.
related_synthesis_entries.title: Average dissipation reaches a statistical obstruction through buffered propagation

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The local propagation estimate is protected by manufactured boundaries: pigeonholing finds gaps at the terminal time, a virial bound keeps them open backward across the short interval, and those persistent gaps limit energy exchange between the finite interior subsystem and its environment. The remaining leakage is charged to preselected multiscale boundary-energy budgets.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Indices j_- and j_+ are chosen inside the log^3 T buffers so their exterior gaps at t2 are at least 1/log T. Lemma 12(iv) and the short time-step restriction keep these gaps comparable throughout [t1,t2]. For K=[j_-,j_+], Lemma 12 bounds the derivative of the unnormalized internal energy by cross-environment terms. Splitting internal pairs according to whether |x_k-x_k'| is at least one bounds the first class directly and the short-pair class by dyadic boundary energies from Proposition 27 plus the ambient energy from Theorem 17. Integration gives E_K(t2) <= E_K(t1) plus the endpoint-displacement cost; monotonicity and Lemma 16 convert this to the claimed renormalized-energy inequality on the shrunken interval.
directed.conceptual_reading: Approximate locality is not assumed; it is created by selecting and preserving buffer gaps. Once the finite subsystem is separated, its failure to be closed is quantified as boundary flux, and a scale decomposition matches that flux to the previously prepared boundary certificate.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The finite-subsystem energy E_K is the bridge object: it has a usable differential inequality even though the desired renormalized energy is localized and reference-subtracted. Persistent boundary gaps connect particle geometry to small environmental flux, while Lemma 16 reconnects E_K to E-tilde on the interior interval.
directed.boundary_or_failure: This is only short-time, approximate local monotonicity. It requires the pigeonholed gaps, the virial persistence estimate, the multiscale-good interval, global integrated-energy control, and a shrunken output interval. Without a buffer, cross-environment denominators can become large and the argument supplies no comparable propagation bound.
directed.uncertainty: The conservation-with-buffer mechanism and final inequality are explicit. The cross-term displays are formula-dense and extraction-sensitive, so exact index restrictions, signs, and dyadic coefficients should be verified before formal or numerical use.

The finite-subsystem energy E_K and its differential upper bound by cross-environment terms are accurately identified as the bridge used to prove local propagation.
The candidate correctly describes the split at |x_k-x_k'|=1, the dyadic boundary-energy control from Proposition 27, the ambient contribution from Theorem 17, and subsequent time integration.
Monotonicity and Lemma 16 do convert the unnormalized finite-subsystem estimate back to the renormalized estimate on the shrunken interval.

Describing the cross-environment contribution as boundary flux is interpretive but grounded in the displayed differential inequality.
